01

The argument

We usually judge how well a country is doing by its income. Yet the relationships around us, at home, at work and in our neighbourhoods, are a large part of what makes life worth living. Researchers call this social capital, and its link with life satisfaction is well established (Putnam, 2000; Helliwell & Putnam, 2004).

The quote on my desk

“Money can't buy happiness”: a maxim argued over since Rousseau's Discourse on the Arts and Sciences ({{rousseau}}). {{since_rousseau}} years later, the data still mostly agrees.

What is less clear is whether it works the same way everywhere. Most studies treat the link as uniform and measure trust, networks and norms with separate instruments. I used the ISSP {{issp}} Social Networks module, an underused survey that captures all three of Putnam's dimensions at once, and tested the link in five very different countries.

The answer: social capital matters everywhere, but not in the same way. Culture and natural risk change which relationships count. Where the state provides more, social capital carries less of the load. And the most consistent link holds in every country: people who trust that the system treats them fairly are more satisfied with life.

02

How I tested it

One survey, five countries, {{n_measures}} measures of social capital and {{n_moderators}} contextual moderators, used to test four hypotheses. The specification:

Tool stack

R: mice, emmeans, car (VIF). Excel for early wrangling. The ISSP codebook as gospel.

Study specification

Data
ISSP {{issp}} Social Networks module, n = {{n_total}}
Outcome
Single {{likert_max}}-point life satisfaction item
Social capital
{{n_measures}} measures: trust (society, fairness, organisations), social networks, support resources (personal, organisational), reciprocity norms (elder care, family first, societal care), contact (daily, organisational)
Governed context
Human Development Index, Social Progress Index, Corruption Perceptions Index, within-country income percentile. The dissertation calls these “explicit” moderators.
Naturally occurring context
INFORM natural-hazard risk; Hofstede's power distance, masculinity and individualism. “Implicit” moderators in the dissertation.
Missing data
MICE, predictive mean matching, grouped by country ({{missing}} of {{n_total}} rows had a gap)
Dimension reduction
PCA, most α ≥ {{alpha}}
Models
Country-level and pooled OLS with interaction terms
Comparisons
Estimated marginal means, Tukey
Diagnostics
VIF, AIC/BIC
Controls
Age, partner status, ISCO-08 skill level, household financial ease
Literatures
Putnam's social capital framework · Hofstede's cultural dimensions · the Easterlin paradox and subjective wellbeing research · Lin's position generator · Van der Gaag & Snijders' resource generator
Quietly proud of

Reconstructing the ISCO-08 skill levels for Chinese agricultural workers, where the ISSP module has a known missing-data issue flagged on p. {{doc_page}} of its own documentation — so the Chinese sample didn't collapse.

03

What I found

The data are a snapshot, not an experiment, so every result here is an association.

Fairness is the strongest constant

H1a· Within countries ·Supported

Within every country, people with more social capital reported higher life satisfaction, extending Putnam's finding well beyond the US. Trust in fairness was the most consistent link, positive and significant in all five countries and strongest in Austria, where its coefficient was more than twice the other four countries'. That fits the “warm glow” of trust that Bjørnskov (2003b) describes in highly developed countries.

My reading

The surprise was organisational support resources, which went with lower satisfaction, the opposite of what I expected. My reading: people may dislike having to rely on institutions for what they need. It took me a week to see it.

Same social capital, different lives

H1b· Between countries ·Supported

Hold social capital at the sample average and life satisfaction still differs between countries, from {{us_emm}} in the US to {{cn_emm}} in China; only {{tukey_pairs}} are statistically level. The relationships that mattered differed too: trust almost everywhere, social networks in South Africa, and societal norms and resources in China.

My reading

In China, guanxi (關係) networks are also how knowledge, licences, projects and careers flow. When social capital is an economic necessity rather than an extra, an average amount may not feel like enough (He & Gebhardt, 2015).

Context changes which ties matter

H2a · H2b·Supported (H2a with nuance)

Two kinds of national context moderated the link. What a country is given, its natural-disaster risk and cultural values, changed which relationships counted. What governments shape, through development, resources and lower corruption, changed how much social capital mattered at all: as the state provided more, most links weakened, while governance quality was itself linked to higher satisfaction.

Money told a quieter story. Relative income had no significant main effect, but household financial ease, a measure of making ends meet, was one of the strongest predictors throughout. Feeling financially stretched mattered; earning more than your neighbours did not.

Overall, this is a very comprehensive study of the relationship between life satisfaction and social capital in various national contexts. It was a pleasure to read this thoughtful analysis.

Dr Anke Plagnol · supervisor
04

What it doesn't show

Because the data are a snapshot, the arrows could point either way: satisfied people may simply invest more in community. A third factor such as personality, which the ISSP doesn't measure, could also drive both. The model explains about a fifth of the variance in life satisfaction (R² ≈ {{r2}}), normal for this literature. Life satisfaction is a single survey item, and China makes up {{cn_share}}% of the pooled sample ({{cn_n}} of {{n_total}}), so pooled estimates lean towards it.

05

The playbook

Four low-cost ideas the findings point to

Context comes first. Because the link depends on culture and institutions, both need to be understood before anyone designs an intervention. These are directions to explore, not proven effects.

P1

Plan together before the flood

Where High natural-disaster risk

Why
In riskier countries, trust and networks counted for less, societal care counted for more, and hazard risk itself was not positively linked to satisfaction (Table 2).
What it could look like
Neighbourhood emergency plans written with residents: who checks on whom, where to meet, who has a car or a generator. Regular street events, drills and shared meals keep the network alive before it's needed, at a fraction of the cost of new flood defences.
The bigger point
Resilience may be social before it is structural.
P2

Pubs as policy

Where Individualistic cultures

Why
Social networks mattered more where there are fewer ready-made in-groups, so people need bridges to others (Table 2).
What it could look like
Treat the places where strangers meet as social infrastructure. Protect community pubs and parks, design employment resource centres as meeting points as well as service desks, and use national sporting events to bring different groups together. Teaching tolerance and inclusivity in schools helps the bridges get used.
The bigger point
Where people meet is already policy, whether or not anyone designs it.
P3

Fairness is infrastructure

Where Everywhere, especially advanced democracies

Why
Trust in fairness was the most consistent link, positive and significant in all five countries (Fig. 2).
What it could look like
Make fairness visible: transparent decision-making, justice that follows through on petty crimes as well as serious ones, fair wage distribution, and social services that are easy to find and use. The dissertation also argues for progressive taxation.
The bigger point
Perceived fairness may be the one form of social capital a government can build directly.
P4

Community over cash

Where Developed societies

Why
Social capital was consistently linked to satisfaction; relative income was not (§03).
What it could look like
Judge development projects partly by what they do for community, counting new shared spaces, local groups and levels of trust alongside jobs and income. Fund community centres, clubs and mutual-aid networks as core development rather than an add-on.
The bigger point
Progress could be measured in connection as well as cash.

The wider lesson for theory is that institutions can only do so much for wellbeing on their own, because culture and physical environment shape how people interact.

06

What's next

This is a small step in a large literature. Next, I would widen the sample beyond five countries and add personality, which predicts the forms of social capital people build (Tulin, Lancee & Volker, 2018) but which the ISSP doesn't measure. I would also develop better measures of social norms. Above all, I would run a longitudinal panel, even just two waves, to separate “social capital comes first” from “satisfied people build social capital”.

These simple relationships: with family, neighbours, colleagues, friends, and broader society have the power to make life worth living.

From the dissertation's conclusion
